title: What actually makes an AI-generated 3D model ready for commercial work?
author: JnoSEPARA
selftext:
I've started thinking that a good-looking AI 3D model and a commercially usable asset are two different things.

A generated model might look great in a preview, but the real test starts when it enters an actual production pipeline.

Before calling an AI-generated asset ready, I'd check:

• **Topology and geometry**: Is the mesh clean, optimized, and suitable for the intended use?  
• **Textures and materials**: Do the PBR maps, UVs, and materials hold up under different lighting conditions?  
• **Rigging and animation**: For characters, do joints deform correctly and can the asset handle real movement?  
• **Engine compatibility**: Does it import properly into Blender, Unity, Unreal, or Godot without major fixes?  
• **Editing flexibility**: Can artists modify the asset without rebuilding everything?

A model being visually impressive is only the first checkpoint. Commercial workflows care about what happens after generation: handoff, cleanup, iteration, and integration. Research on production-ready AI 3D generation also highlights that usable assets need to go beyond appearance and address geometry, topology, UVs, materials, rigging, and downstream engine requirements.

I've been experimenting with V2Fun because it focuses on more of the workflow around generation, including texturing, retopology, rigging, motion testing, and export, which makes it easier to validate an asset before investing more production time.

For creators using AI-generated assets commercially, what's your minimum requirement before calling a model "ready"?

Clean mesh, perfect textures, working rig, engine import, or something else?

comments.author: buzzspinner
comments.body: How do you compare to meshy and tripo3d

replies.author: Rough_Acanthisitta59
replies.body: If we're talking more than just generation quality but a production ready sense, I'd probably put meshy a bit head as it has more of the stuff I'd actually want after getting a model, like remeshing, rigging, or direct engine integrations.

comments.author: imnotabot303
comments.body:
To be fair most people using AI generated models in games are doing so because they lack 3D modelling knowledge and skill so they have almost no standards.

Anyone who's experienced enough with 3D is much better off just making the model from scratch themselves and just using AI for reference or inspiration.

I attempted to see how good AI was to make something like a game ready vehicle a few months back. I ended up just remodeling the entire thing and used the 3D gen just as a 3D reference.

replies.author: Lavio00
replies.body:
Meh, not sure I agree. I think mesh generation can work quite well. It’s tedius to create a mesh and you can get 80% of the way with AI. Easier to clean a existing mesh than building a new one. Rigging (on humanoids) is a non-issue.

The real problems are any sort of texture work, baking and animations. Retopology is also a craft that’s hard to just intuit without experience, but it’s one that’s easier to get right than the others.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body: It depends on your skill level and the level of polish someone wants. If you only have basic 3D skills then it could be quicker for some ok results but any competent 3D artist will probably find themselves spending more time doing fixes and cleanup than doing it correctly to begin with. Same with rigging and animation. It can be fast if you're just going to use an auto rigger and then slap on some Miximo animations but if you want something more it's still going to take time and skill, especially when it comes to animating.

replies.author: Lavio00
replies.body: Yeah so I guess at the end of the day it seems we agree that low budget/small scale games can absolutely benefit here.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
I don't think it's down to that, it's more down to the skill level of the people using it. Just because a game is small it doesn't mean it needs to be sloppy or low effort. 

At the moment I would say AI 3D gen is most useful as models to use for prototyping.

comments.author: Civil_Log_7536
comments.body:
For characters, I think the quickest reality check is what happens after rigging.

A mesh can look clean, have decent uvs, and still fall apart the second you throw a basic walk cycle to it. Shoulders, knees usually tell you pretty fast if the topology is usable or just looks goood in a static preview.

I don't expect zero cleanup but I don't want to rebuild half the asset after generation either and that's where I draw the line between nice output and game usable

replies.author: Early-Act-6037
replies.body:
Yeah,that is pretty muchhow I look at it too.The animation test usually tells me more than starting at the static mesh for another ten minutes.
I havetried a few of the main AI 3D tools,and forthis kind of workflow I find meshy is convenient.I can remesh the model,rig it,throw on a quick walk or run animation,and then see where the deformation actually starts breaking before deciding what  needs fixing.
I got good results fromtripo too,but I still end up doing the same kind ofchecking and cleanup afterward.I don't think any of these are reallyat the "generate it and forget it" stage yet.
